keyVerseText: If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself: if he were married , then his wife shall go out with him. by himself: Heb. with his body
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun גַּף (gaph) derives from an unused root meaning 'to arch,' which suggests a concept of curvature or elevation. This etymological insight enriches the word's semantic range beyond the usual English glosses, indicating not only a physical part of the body but also an idea of height or elevated place. Thus, the root sense connects the tangible 'body' with the spatial notion of 'height' or 'highest places,' reflecting a layered meaning that encompasses both the physical self and a position of prominence or elevation.
usageInScripture: The word גַּף appears only four times in Scripture, where it consistently conveys either the idea of 'body' or 'self'—especially in the phrase translated as 'by himself'—or the concept of 'height' or 'elevation.' Most frequently, it is rendered 'by himself' (three occurrences), emphasizing the individual's own body or presence, as seen in the legal context of Exodus 21:3. In one instance, it is translated as 'upon,' reflecting its use to denote a spatial height or elevated place, such as in Proverbs 9:3. This limited but focused usage underscores the word’s dual semantic fields of personal embodiment and spatial elevation.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גַּף as both 'body' and 'height' invites a richer theological reflection on the unity of the physical self and its standing before God. The notion of 'by himself' highlights personal responsibility and individuality in covenant and legal contexts, reminding believers that each person stands accountable before God. The aspect of 'height' or 'elevation' can symbolically point to God's exalted position and the believer's call to spiritual elevation. Together, these meanings encourage a holistic view of faith that embraces both our embodied existence and our calling to live elevated in Christ’s righteousness.
keyVerseReflection: Exodus 21:3 states, 'If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself,' where גַּף emphasizes the individual's own body or self. The phrase 'by himself' highlights the personal nature of the slave’s legal status and freedom, underscoring that the person enters and exits the covenantal arrangement in their own right. This use of גַּף brings clarity to the verse, stressing the integrity and individuality of the person involved, which aligns with the broader biblical theme of personal responsibility before God.
